content: 1. Abrupt discontinuation of certain beta-blocking agents has been associated with exacerbations of angina pectoris and, in some cases, myocardial infarction. 2. When discontinuing metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets in patients with ischemic heart disease, the dosage should be gradually reduced over 1-2 weeks, and the patient should be closely monitored. 3. 4. Patients should be advised not to interrupt or discontinue therapy without consulting their physician. 5. Since coronary artery disease is common and may be unrecognized, abrupt discontinuation of metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets should be avoided, even in patients treated only for hypertension. 6. Metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets are indicated for the treatment of hypertension and may be used alone or in combination with other antihypertensive agents. 7. These tablets are also indicated for the long-term treatment of angina pectoris to reduce angina attacks and improve exercise tolerance. 8. Metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets are indicated for the treatment of stable, symptomatic heart failure (NYHA Class II or III) of ischemic, hypertensive, or cardiomyopathic origin. 9. In heart failure patients, metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets have been shown to reduce the rate of mortality and hospitalizations, primarily through a reduction in cardiovascular mortality and heart failure-related hospitalizations. 10. 11. Dosages above 400 mg per day have not been studied. 12. 13. Metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets are not recommended for pediatric patients under 6 years of age. 14. In elderly patients, a lower initial starting dose is recommended due to the higher likelihood of reduced hepatic, renal, or cardiac function and concomitant diseases or therapies. 15. Metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets are contraindicated in patients with severe bradycardia, secondor third-degree heart block, cardiogenic shock, decompensated cardiac failure, sick sinus syndrome (without a pacemaker), and hypersensitivity to any component of the product. 16. Beta-blockers, including metoprolol, may mask symptoms of hypoglycemia, such as tachycardia, and should be used cautiously in diabetic patients. 17. Patients with bronchospastic diseases should generally avoid beta-blockers, but metoprolol may be used with caution at the lowest effective dose, along with readily available bronchodilators. 18. In patients with pheochromocytoma, metoprolol should only be used in combination with an alpha-blocker and after alpha-blockade has been initiated. 19. Beta-blockers may exacerbate symptoms of arterial insufficiency in patients with peripheral vascular disease. 20. Metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets should not be abruptly discontinued prior to major surgery, as this may impair the heart's ability to respond to reflex adrenergic stimuli. 21. Adverse reactions commonly reported include tiredness, dizziness, depression, diarrhea, shortness of breath, bradycardia, and rash. 22. Overdosage of metoprolol may result in severe bradycardia, hypotension, cardiogenic shock, AV block, heart failure, bronchospasm, hypoxia, and impaired consciousness. Intensive care and consultation with a poison control center are recommended in such cases. 23. Metoprolol succinate is a beta1-selective adrenergic receptor blocker that reduces heart rate and cardiac output at rest and during exercise, inhibits isoproterenol-induced tachycardia, and decreases reflex orthostatic tachycardia. 24. The drug is metabolized by the liver, and its blood levels may increase significantly in patients with impaired hepatic function, necessitating lower initial doses and gradual titration. 25. 26. 27. Safety and efficacy in patients under 6 years of age have not been established. 28. In elderly patients, no notable differences in efficacy or adverse reaction rates were observed compared to younger patients, but lower initial doses are recommended. 29. Metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets are formulated to provide controlled and predictable release for once-daily administration. 30. The mechanism of the antihypertensive effects of beta-blockers is not fully understood but may involve decreased cardiac output, reduced sympathetic outflow, and suppression of renin activity.
